name: Sogou C++ Workflow (HTTP Server)
workload: Minimal HTTP server returning a fixed-content body; QPS and latency measured across concurrency 1-2048 and body sizes 16B-64KB using wrk/wrk2, compared against nginx (40 worker processes) and brpc (40 threads).
claimed_speedup: Consistently higher QPS and lower latency than nginx across all tested concurrency/body-size combinations; text states it 'can maintain 500K QPS' at 64B/512B body sizes under sufficient concurrency
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.8.5 (optimization flags not specified on page)
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon E5-2630 v4 (40 cores total), 192GB RAM, 25Gbps NIC, CentOS 7.8.2003, kernel 3.10.0-1127
tradeoffs: Task/series-based async programming model has a learning curve vs simple thread-per-request servers.
caveats: Benchmark is first-party (workflow's own repo); most curves are only shown as images, the ~500K QPS peak is the only figure stated in prose; nginx/brpc tuning (40 workers/threads) was chosen by the workflow authors and may not be optimal for the comparison targets.

name: Lwan
workload: TechEmpower Framework Benchmarks Round 10 JSON-serialization test, Peak Hosting dual-Xeon E5 environment with 10-gigabit Ethernet.
claimed_speedup: Lwan ranked #1 ('took the crown') in Round 10's Peak-environment JSON test, part of a >100% jump in the round's top score vs Round 9 (2.2M vs 1.05M req/s); the blog post separately states Go's entries fell out of the Peak environment's top-10 that round
hardware: Peak Hosting dual-Xeon E5 servers, 10 Gigabit Ethernet (exact CPU model not given in this post)
tradeoffs: Hand-written HTTP parser and coroutine-based design trade some safety/portability guarantees for speed; GPLv2 is more restrictive than nginx's license for some users.
caveats: Benchmark is from April 2015 (TFB Round 10) on hardware/software stacks retired long ago; not re-verified on current Lwan or current Go; the 'crown' is specifically the JSON-serialization/Peak-environment ranking, not every test type in that round.
found_via: HN Algolia query 'lwan web server' -> lwan.ws homepage FAQ linking to the TechEmpower Round 10 blog post

name: H2O
workload: 612-byte static file serving on two Amazon EC2 c3.8xlarge instances (server+client), 250 concurrent clients, wrk (HTTP/1) and h2load (HTTP/2), nginx open_file_cache enabled vs H2O's built-in file cache; also a first-paint/download-completion comparison over a simulated 8Mbps/100ms-latency network.
claimed_speedup: Charts show H2O completing the static-file benchmark faster than nginx and reaching first-paint/full-download sooner than nginx on the simulated slow network; exact requests/sec and millisecond values are shown only as embedded PNG chart images, not as numbers in the page text
tradeoffs: H2O's open-file-cache trades memory for lower file-serving latency; HTTP/3 and mruby scripting add complexity vs nginx.
caveats: Benchmark page itself calls the reverse-proxy chart 'old'; the static-file chart carries no visible date but the page appears essentially unchanged since ~2015; numbers are only visible in chart images, not extractable as text; no compiler/build flags stated for either server.
found_via: GitHub: h2o/h2o README -> project website h2o.examp1e.net/benchmarks.html

name: Tempesta FW
workload: 600-byte static file HTTP/1.1 GET with 'Connection: close', wrk load generator, VM-to-VM (KVM/virtio) and hardware-to-VM (macvtap) configurations at 1/2/4 vCPUs.
claimed_speedup: Requests/sec read directly from the page: 1 vCPU VM-to-VM 13947.89 (Tempesta) vs 13489.36 (nginx), ~1.03x; 2 vCPU 41775.59 vs 18727.89, ~2.23x; hardware-to-VM 1 vCPU 25140.11 vs 19644.42, ~1.28x. README separately claims 'up to 1.8M HTTP requests per second... x3 faster than Nginx or HAProxy' on unspecified hardware.
hardware: 2x Intel Xeon E3-1240v5 (4c/8t), 32GB RAM, Mellanox ConnectX-2 10Gbps NIC; Debian 9.12 / Ubuntu 16.04.6 guests under KVM
tradeoffs: Runs as a Linux kernel module, which raises operational/security/portability costs compared to a userspace server like nginx; tied to GPLv2 kernel licensing.
caveats: Vendor's own (first-party) benchmark; compiler/optimization flags for building nginx or Tempesta not stated; speedup is inconsistent across configurations (~1.03x-1.3x at 1 vCPU vs ~2.2x at 2 vCPU); the page itself flags virtualization as an imperfect testbed for small-packet workloads; the headline README figure ('3x faster, 1.8M req/s') is not sourced to this same detailed page.
found_via: GitHub: tempesta-tech/tempesta README 'x3 faster than Nginx' claim -> linked knowledge-base Performance / HTTP-transactions-performance pages

name: Drogon
workload: GET / route benchmarked in isolated Docker containers at concurrency 64/256/512 using the oha load generator (the-benchmarker/web-frameworks reproducible suite).
claimed_speedup: Drogon 1.9: 126.4K-135.0K req/s across concurrency 64-512 vs Go net/http ('nethttp' 1.22): 67.2K-71.5K req/s -> roughly 1.8x-2x higher throughput at every tested concurrency level
compiler_and_flags: Debian trixie-slim + build-essential (default gcc/g++; the benchmark's own CMakeLists.txt sets no explicit -O flags or CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE)
hardware: Benchmark host metadata reports 16 vCPUs, Linux 7.2.6-200.fc44 x86_64, containerized/shared runner (per-container CPU allocation not separately documented)
tradeoffs: Full-featured framework (ORM, views, sessions, plugins) adds binary size/complexity vs a bare net/http server; still well behind actix-web (163K-179K req/s) in the same suite.
caveats: No explicit compiler optimization flags in the benchmark's own CMakeLists.txt; the dataset's hardware label ('M1 Eight-Core Processor' on a reported Linux x86_64 host) looks like a data-entry artifact, so the exact CPU model is uncertain. A separate single-author benchmark (gonwan/webframework-benchmark, AMD 7840HS host, wrk) also shows Drogon 1.8.7 at 320k/s beating Boost.Beast 1.83 at 220k/s, though slightly behind nginx (336k/s) in that same test.
found_via: GitHub: drogonframework/drogon README link to TechEmpower results -> cross-checked against the-benchmarker/web-frameworks data.json (cpp/drogon)

name: Oat++
workload: Same the-benchmarker/web-frameworks containerized GET / benchmark as Drogon, concurrency 64/256/512, oha load generator.
claimed_speedup: oatpp 1.3: 98.2K-115.7K req/s vs Go net/http 67.2K-71.5K req/s -> roughly 1.4x-1.7x higher throughput
compiler_and_flags: Debian trixie-slim + build-essential (default gcc/g++; no explicit optimization flags set in the benchmark's CMakeLists.txt)
hardware: Same shared benchmark host as the Drogon entry: 16 vCPUs, Linux x86_64 container host
tradeoffs: Throughput degrades somewhat as concurrency rises (115.7K at c=64 down to 98.2K at c=512), unlike Go/Drogon which stay flatter; zero-dependency design trades some convenience features for portability.
caveats: Same shared-host/compiler-flag caveats as the Drogon entry from this suite. oatpp's own site benchmarks (e.g. '5 Million WebSockets') do not name a baseline and so do not qualify on their own.
found_via: GitHub: the-benchmarker/web-frameworks cpp/oatpp directory and data.json metrics

name: CWIST
workload: Same the-benchmarker/web-frameworks containerized GET / benchmark, concurrency 64/256/512, oha load generator.
claimed_speedup: CWIST: 148.7K-154.7K req/s vs Go net/http 67.2K-71.5K req/s -> roughly 2.1x-2.2x higher throughput
hardware: Same shared benchmark host as the Drogon/oatpp entries: 16 vCPUs, Linux x86_64 container host
tradeoffs: Very new/low-adoption project (15 stars); a large feature surface (HTTP/3, WebTransport, post-quantum crypto) for a project this young raises production-hardening questions.
caveats: Extremely low star count and no independent track record; the only evidence found this session is this one third-party container benchmark.

name: Agoo-C
workload: Same the-benchmarker/web-frameworks containerized GET / benchmark, concurrency 64/256/512, oha load generator.
claimed_speedup: agoo-c: 75.0K req/s at concurrency 64, rising to 141.4K-149.2K req/s at concurrency 256/512, vs Go net/http's flat 67.2K-71.5K req/s -> roughly on par at c=64 and up to ~2.1x higher at c=256/512
hardware: Same shared benchmark host as the Drogon/oatpp/CWIST entries: 16 vCPUs, Linux x86_64 container host
tradeoffs: Unmaintained since ~2020; C API only, so C++ use requires wrapping; only roughly ties Go net/http at the lowest tested concurrency.
caveats: No commits since December 2020, so the binary tested may be an old/frozen build; the jump from 75.0K req/s at c=64 to ~145K at c=256/512 is an unusual scaling curve worth independent re-verification.

name: libevhtp
workload: Single plaintext-response endpoint in a 4-core Docker environment, wrk -c1000 -t10 -d30s with HTTP keep-alive, client running on a 12-core AMD 7840HS host.
claimed_speedup: libevhtp 1.2.18 (on libevent 2.1.12): 254k req/s vs Boost.Beast 1.83: 220k req/s -> about 1.15x higher throughput (both below nginx 336k/s and Drogon 320k/s in the same table)
hardware: 4-core Docker containers on a 12-core AMD 7840HS host, LinuxMint 22.3 / Ubuntu 24.04, Docker userland-proxy disabled
tradeoffs: C API (needs a C++ wrapper for idiomatic use); depends on libevent; archived by GitHub as read-only.
caveats: Single-author 'homemade' benchmark (0-star benchmark repo, not independently reviewed); compiler flags not stated; libevhtp itself has been archived/unmaintained since ~2019-2021.
found_via: GitHub: CrowCpp/Crow README benchmark links -> guteksan/REST-CPP-benchmark search led to gonwan/webframework-benchmark comparison table

name: UCall (formerly UJRPC)
workload: JSON-RPC 'sum' endpoint; latency measured with 1 client, throughput with 32 concurrent clients; UCall (POSIX and io_uring backends) vs FastAPI over REST/WebSocket and gRPC, on AWS c7g.metal (Graviton 3), Ubuntu 22.10.
claimed_speedup: UCall POSIX (C): 62us latency / 79,000 rps; UCall io_uring (C): 22us latency / 231,000 rps -- vs FastAPI over REST (Python): 1,203us latency / 3,184 rps -- roughly 25x-70x higher throughput and ~19x-55x lower latency depending on backend
tradeoffs: io_uring backend requires Linux 5.19+; C API is lower-level than FastAPI's Python ergonomics; JSON-RPC rather than full REST semantics.
caveats: README does not state whether FastAPI/uvicorn was run with uvloop installed, so the baseline is recorded as 'FastAPI (uvicorn/asyncio)' rather than uvloop itself and marked baseline_in_list=false; first-party benchmark, no compiler flags given; not updated in about a year.
found_via: GitHub: gh search repos 'uvloop language:C++' turned up unrelated hits; broadened to 'faster than FastAPI' style C libraries -> unum-cloud/UCall (formerly ujrpc)

name: Crow
workload: TechEmpower-style /json plaintext test reusing TechEmpower/FrameworkBenchmarks' own Go implementation code, on AWS c3.8xlarge with an 8-core wrk load generator, concurrency 16-16384.
claimed_speedup: Crow: 136.3K-296.7K req/s across concurrency 16-16384 vs Go (net/http, TFB reference code): 92.9K-180.5K req/s -> roughly 1.3x-1.7x higher throughput at every concurrency level tested (e.g. 296.7K vs 180.5K at concurrency 4096, ~1.64x)
hardware: AWS EC2 c3.8xlarge (server), 8-core load generator running wrk
tradeoffs: Header-only, largely synchronous-style API (native async listed as still in development in the current README); comparison used an older Go/TFB implementation that may not reflect modern Go net/http tuning.
caveats: Benchmark repo (ipkn/crow-benchmark) dates to ~2015-2018 and is first-party (made by Crow's original author); results live only in a linked Google Sheet/chart, not in the benchmark repo's own text; no compiler flags or exact CPU model (only the 'c3.8xlarge' instance type) are stated; not re-run on current Crow or Go versions.
found_via: GitHub: CrowCpp/Crow README -> linked ipkn/crow-benchmark repo -> linked Google Sheets results (exported as CSV)

name: CPV Framework
workload: Plaintext-style endpoint, wrk/wrk2, server pinned to 1-2 cores via taskset, 100-20000 connections, on an Intel Xeon E31225 @3.10GHz (4 cores).
claimed_speedup: cpv-framework 0.2.0.0 vs actix-web 2.0.0: 84.7K vs 80.5K req/s (1 core, 100 conns, ~1.05x); 170.6K vs 149.6K req/s (2 cores, 100 conns, ~1.14x); 76.6K vs 71.2K req/s (1 core, 10000 conns, ~1.08x); at 2 cores/10000 conns cpv-framework was slightly slower than actix-web (136.7K vs 141.5K)
tradeoffs: Built on Seastar's shared-nothing/thread-per-core model, which requires restructuring app code around that model; wins over actix-web are marginal (~5-14%) and inconsistent across configurations.
caveats: First-party wiki benchmark from January 2020 comparing against actix-web 2.0.0 (now several major versions old); project has had no commits since; no compiler flags stated; cpv-framework loses to actix-web in the 2-core/10000-connection case, showing the win is not universal.
found_via: GitHub: scylladb/seastar README 'Projects using Seastar' -> cpv-project/cpv-framework README -> linked wiki Benchmark-Results page
